strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting: improving quality and generalization while avoiding the huge Gaussian counts of per-pixel methods. The compact 16x subsampled representation plus recurrent refinement is a sensible design for scaling to high-resolution, multi-view inputs.

The empirical results are strong. On DL3DV with 8 views at 512x960, ReSplat reports clearly better PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS than retrained 3DGS, MVSplat, and DepthSplat while using far fewer Gaussians and rendering faster. The 16-view DL3DV and 2-view RealEstate10K evaluations broaden the evidence beyond a single benchmark.

The ablations are useful and support the main architectural choices: kNN/global attention for compact initialization, the rendering-error feedback signal, feature-space error, and compression factor tradeoffs. The generalization plots across dataset and resolution are also a valuable diagnostic for the recurrent mechanism.

The method is clearly presented, with a coherent pipeline and enough implementation detail to understand the model, training stages, recurrence, losses, and evaluation settings. The stated intent to release code, pretrained models, and scripts is positive for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but not transformative: learned iterative/recurrent refinement and learned optimizers are well established, and the paper’s main innovation is adapting these ideas to feed-forward Gaussian splatting with rendering-error feedback. This is valuable, but the conceptual leap is moderate.

Some claims about the recurrent model are overstated. In Table 1, the iteration-0 model already achieves 26.21 PSNR, while three recurrent iterations improve to 26.82; most of the gain over DepthSplat appears to come from the stronger compact initialization architecture rather than recurrence itself. The paper should more carefully separate the contributions of compact initialization, backbone/training changes, and recurrent updates.

The fairness of comparisons is imperfect in places. Long-LRM numbers are borrowed because weights are unavailable, and the training/evaluation protocol may differ. For RealEstate10K, the method changes to 4x subsampling with four Gaussians per point, so the central 16x compactness claim does not apply in that setting.

The generalization evidence is promising but limited: the cross-dataset and cross-resolution plots mainly compare different recurrent iterations of the proposed model, rather than directly showing competing methods under the same distribution shifts. This weakens the claim that ReSplat is robust relative to prior feed-forward models.

Reproducibility may be challenging despite the planned release, because training requires very large compute, e.g. 16 GH200 GPUs for multiple 80K-step stages on DL3DV and 300K steps for RealEstate10K. More detail on data splits, target-view sampling, memory use, and exact runtime accounting would help.

The limitations section is honest about kNN scaling and saturation after three iterations, but the paper could discuss failure cases more concretely, such as thin structures, reflective/transparent regions, pose noise, and cases where fixed Gaussian counts limit reconstruction quality.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting: improving quality and generalization without per-scene optimization. The combination of compact Gaussian initialization and recurrent refinement from rendering-error feedback is practically relevant for sparse-view novel view synthesis.

The empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks. On DL3DV with 8 views, ReSplat substantially improves over MVSplat/DepthSplat while using far fewer Gaussians and faster rendering; the 16-view DL3DV and 2-view RealEstate10K results also show competitive or state-of-the-art numbers.

The ablations are useful and generally support the main design choices: kNN/global attention for compact initialization, rendering-error feedback for recurrence, and the speed/quality tradeoff from the compression factor.

The paper is mostly clear and well structured, with a readable pipeline figure and a concise limitations section that acknowledges the kNN attention bottleneck and saturation after a few recurrent steps.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate rather than high. Learned iterative refinement, feedback from rendering/reconstruction error, and recurrent learned optimization are well-established ideas; the main contribution is an engineering synthesis for Gaussian splats rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

Some claims are overstated. The manuscript says the feedback signal 'naturally adapts to unseen data distributions at test time,' but the method does not perform test-time learning or optimization; it feeds input-view errors into a trained network. The evidence for out-of-distribution robustness is limited and mostly shown as iteration curves, not a broad comparison against baselines under the same shifts.

Comparison fairness is not fully convincing. ReSplat uses a large ViT-B depth backbone and substantial progressive training on 16 GH200 GPUs, while several baselines are borrowed from prior work or retrained under unclear capacity/training-budget matching. Long-LRM comparisons are especially hard to interpret because weights are unavailable and results are borrowed.

The reported efficiency story is mixed. Rendering is faster due to fewer Gaussians, but reconstruction time is slower than some feed-forward baselines and Long-LRM in key settings. The paper emphasizes 100x faster than 3DGS, but this is expected for feed-forward methods and less informative than comparisons to contemporary feed-forward models with matched hardware and implementation.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the code-release promise. Important hyperparameters such as learning rates, batch sizes, target-view sampling, exact dataset splits/protocols, and memory/computation costs are not sufficiently specified for a high-compute system paper.

The recurrent improvement saturates quickly and is relatively small in the main high-resolution table after initialization, suggesting that much of the gain may come from the stronger compact initialization rather than the recurrent mechanism. The paper could better disentangle backbone capacity, initialization design, and recurrence.

Visual evidence is limited and selected. Failure cases, challenging camera motions, sparse/low-overlap inputs, dynamic content, or inaccurate poses are not analyzed, leaving uncertainty about robustness beyond the reported benchmark settings.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely Algorithms/General contribution for generalizable view synthesis: a feed-forward recurrent 3D Gaussian splatting model that uses input-view rendering error as a learned feedback signal for iterative, gradient-free refinement.

The main idea is technically well motivated. Combining a compact 16x-subsampled Gaussian initialization with recurrent updates addresses both scalability and the single-pass limitation of existing feed-forward Gaussian methods.

Experimental results are strong across several relevant settings. On DL3DV with 8 views at 512x960, ReSplat improves substantially over MVSplat, DepthSplat, and sparse-view 3DGS while using far fewer Gaussians and faster rendering; it also shows competitive results for 16-view DL3DV and 2-view RealEstate10K.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: kNN/global attention matter for compact initialization, rendering error is essential for recurrent improvement, and feature-space error improves perceptual metrics.
The paper makes a credible case for improved robustness under dataset and resolution shift, which is an important practical advantage over single-step feed-forward models.
The manuscript is mostly clear, with an understandable pipeline, implementation details, limitations, and a stated intent to release code and pretrained models.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental rather than foundational: recurrent learned optimization and feedback-based refinement are well established in vision, and the paper’s contribution is mainly a strong adaptation to feed-forward Gaussian splatting rather than a fundamentally new recurrent optimization principle.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled. For the 16-view DL3DV setting, several baseline numbers are borrowed from Long-LRM, and Long-LRM weights are unavailable; this makes the fairness of speed, training setup, and evaluation details harder to verify.

The method is computationally heavy to train, requiring up to 16 GH200 GPUs over multiple long stages. This raises reproducibility concerns, despite the promised code release, and may limit practical adoption by smaller labs.

The recurrent gains saturate quickly after about three iterations, and the paper does not deeply analyze why longer test-time compute fails to help or how the fixed Gaussian set constrains refinement.

The efficiency story is mixed: rendering is faster due to fewer Gaussians, but reconstruction time can be slower than some feed-forward baselines because of kNN and attention operations. The paper acknowledges this, but more detailed memory/runtime scaling analysis would strengthen the claim of scalability.

Generalization evidence is promising but still limited to a small number of dataset/resolution shifts. More diverse real-world scenes, camera noise, pose errors, and unposed or imperfect-calibration settings would better establish robustness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting: improving quality and generalization while avoiding per-scene optimization and the large Gaussian counts of per-pixel predictors.

The main idea is technically well motivated: a compact Gaussian initialization followed by a weight-sharing recurrent update network driven by input-view rendering error. This is a natural and useful bridge between single-pass feed-forward reconstruction and iterative optimization.

The empirical results are strong across several settings. On DL3DV with 8 views at 512x960, ReSplat substantially outperforms 3DGS, MVSplat, and DepthSplat while using far fewer Gaussians than per-pixel feed-forward baselines and faster rendering. It also compares favorably to Long-LRM in the 16-view setting and performs well on RealEstate10K/ACID.

The ablations are thoughtful and support the main design choices, including rendering-error feedback, recurrent hidden state, kNN/global attention, coordinate-frame choice, compression factors, and recurrent versus non-recurrent variants.
The paper is generally clear, with a coherent method description, useful profiling, and visual comparisons. The appendix adds meaningful evidence rather than only extra qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is solid but not entirely surprising given prior learned-optimization and recurrent refinement work, including G3R and DeepView. The paper distinguishes itself by being gradient-free and feed-forward from sparse posed images, but the relationship to gradient-based learned refinement could be empirically stronger, e.g. with more direct comparisons beyond 3DGS optimization from the same initialization.

The strongest claims about generalization are partly supported by plots rather than full quantitative tables and appear limited to related posed video-style datasets. The method still assumes accurate camera poses and a video/COLMAP-like coordinate setup, so its robustness under pose noise, unordered image collections, wider baselines, or non-video capture is not established.

The method uses very large training resources and a large initialization backbone, while the recurrent module is small. The paper reports inference profiling, but gives limited discussion of training cost, memory scaling, and whether the gains mainly come from the stronger initialization/training recipe versus the recurrent mechanism.

Some comparisons have caveats: Long-LRM numbers are borrowed due to unavailable weights, the SplatFormer comparison required substantial adaptation and may not be fully representative, and the 2-view RealEstate10K setup changes the compression design so it no longer demonstrates the same Gaussian-count advantage.

The recurrent refinement saturates after four iterations, and the paper does not deeply analyze failure cases or cases where input-view reconstruction feedback might improve training-view consistency without improving novel-view geometry. The limitations section acknowledges scalability but remains brief on these behavioral risks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in feed-forward 3D Gaussian splatting: improving sparse-view reconstruction quality while reducing the very large Gaussian counts used by per-pixel prediction methods.

The core design is technically coherent: a compact 16x subsampled Gaussian initialization is followed by weight-shared recurrent updates driven by input-view rendering error. The use of rendering error as a learned feedback signal is a reasonable and useful adaptation of learned-optimization ideas to generalizable Gaussian splatting.

Experimental results are broad and mostly strong. The paper evaluates 8-view and 16-view DL3DV settings, 2-view RealEstate10K, cross-dataset ACID generalization, different resolutions, different view counts, optimization-based baselines, and multiple ablations. The reported gains over MVSplat/DepthSplat and 3DGS in sparse-view DL3DV are substantial.

The efficiency story is compelling in the main 8-view setting: ReSplat uses far fewer Gaussians than per-pixel feed-forward baselines and has faster rendering, while recurrent refinement improves quality monotonically with a modest runtime increase.
The ablations support the main architectural choices, especially the importance of rendering-error feedback, recurrent state, kNN attention, and the compact initialization strategy.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental rather than foundational. Recurrent learned refinement, learned optimization, rendering-error feedback, point/attention updates, and feed-forward Gaussian prediction all have close precedents; the contribution is mainly a well-engineered combination for this setting.

Some comparisons are not fully satisfying. The optimization-based 3DGS baselines are disadvantaged in sparse-view settings without stronger sparse-view regularization, while learned methods benefit from large-scale training priors. The appendix adds a depth-regularized variant, but it is still not a direct comparison to several specialized sparse-view 3DGS methods with their full published pipelines.

Reproducibility remains a concern. The paper promises code and pretrained model release, but the project page is blank in the manuscript. Training requires very large compute, e.g. 16 GH200 GPUs across multiple long stages, making independent verification difficult without released checkpoints and exact scripts.

The paper does not deeply analyze failure cases. It reports strong aggregate metrics, but gives limited discussion of when recurrent updates degrade geometry, how the method behaves under pose noise, dynamic objects, non-video capture, unbounded scenes, exposure changes, or inaccurate COLMAP poses.

The claimed generalization is suggestive but not fully quantified in the main text. Several cross-dataset, cross-resolution, and cross-view results are shown mainly as plots without complete numeric tables or comparisons to other baselines under the same distribution shifts.

The 2-view RealEstate10K setup changes the representation by using 4x subsampling and decoding multiple Gaussians per point, so it no longer demonstrates the same Gaussian-count reduction emphasized in the main DL3DV contribution.

The method remains dependent on posed input images and a depth-prediction backbone, but the limitations section focuses mostly on kNN attention scalability and saturation after four iterations rather than these broader deployment constraints.

Presentation has minor polish issues, including grammatical errors, an empty project-page placeholder, and some dense figure/table formatting. These do not invalidate the work but weaken confidence in readiness.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and well-motivated Algorithms/General contribution: a recurrent feed-forward Gaussian splatting model that uses rendering error as feedback to iteratively refine compact Gaussian representations without explicit gradient computation.

The empirical results are strong. On DL3DV, ReSplat substantially improves over MVSplat, DepthSplat, and vanilla 3DGS in the 8-view high-resolution setting, while using far fewer Gaussians and achieving faster rendering. The gains are consistent across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

The compact initialization is practically important. Predicting Gaussians in a 16x subsampled 3D space directly addresses a real scalability bottleneck of per-pixel feed-forward Gaussian methods, and the paper shows a convincing speed/quality trade-off through compression-factor ablations.

The ablation study is unusually thorough: rendering-error variants, coordinate frames, kNN/global attention in both the initialization and recurrent modules, recurrent vs non-recurrent architectures, feature choices for error computation, and runtime profiling are all analyzed.

The generalization experiments across datasets, resolutions, and view counts support the central claim that recurrent feedback improves robustness beyond a single feed-forward pass. The ACID zero-shot and cross-resolution results are especially relevant.

The method is clearly described, with useful implementation details, training schedules, parameter counts, profiling, and limitations. The promised release of code, pretrained models, and scripts would make the work reproducible if fulfilled.
weaknesses: The core idea is compelling but not conceptually radical: it combines known learned iterative refinement ideas with feed-forward Gaussian splatting. The novelty lies more in the system design and empirical validation than in a fundamentally new optimization principle.

The evaluation depends heavily on known camera poses and video-style datasets with COLMAP poses. The paper does not deeply explore robustness to pose noise, calibration errors, wide-baseline non-video captures, dynamic content, or very large unbounded scenes, which limits the scope of the generalization claims.

Some comparisons are imperfect. Long-LRM numbers are partly borrowed because weights are unavailable, SplatFormer is difficult to adapt and the comparison may not be fully representative, and sparse-view 3DGS baselines may not cover the strongest possible regularized optimization pipelines.

The approach remains computationally heavy to train, requiring many GH200 GPU runs, and the main model has 223M parameters. This raises practical reproducibility concerns despite the planned code release.

The recurrent update saturates after about four iterations and still relies on costly kNN point attention. The paper acknowledges this, but it weakens claims about scalable test-time compute, especially for larger scenes or more than 500K Gaussians.

The method uses input-view rendering error as the feedback signal, so it is less clear how well the recurrence improves geometry or appearance in target regions that are poorly constrained or occluded in the input views. More analysis of failure cases and novel-view geometry consistency would strengthen the paper.

In some settings the advantage is more nuanced than the headline results suggest: for 32 views in the appendix, 3DGS has higher PSNR than ReSplat, and on two-view RealEstate10K ReSplat roughly matches but does not dominate the strongest LVSM variant on all metrics.
